sourceTitleEn: Exaggerate to Make Up for Information Loss

reviewEvidence.transcriptCaveat: Browser transcript export was unavailable. Official on-picture English captions were sampled every 0.5 seconds throughout the 148-second video, deduplicated and read in full. Minor OCR artefacts are retained in the raw file. This is not an independently checked Japanese audio transcription.
reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Full-duration six-second contact sheets inspected, including the Clock Tower 3 cutscene, Ultra Street Fighter IV and Elden Ring examples; not continuous audio or every-frame review.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: Why can a believable real-world performance become weak after it is transferred into a game?
thesis: A game character loses some of the information available from a real person. Amplify the readable performance according to the character's screen size, genre and controls so the intended action survives that loss.

claims: Clock Tower 3 provides an example of deliberately conspicuous cutscene performances.
A performance that appears exaggerated in isolation can be a useful starting point for asking what information the medium conveys.
sections.observedVisuals: Clock Tower 3 cover/context card followed by several broad character gestures in a room.
exampleRoles: Clock Tower 3 is the central low-detail-character acting example, not a claim that older games are superior.
sections.personalAttribution: The source introduces director Kinji Fukasaku and his final work. That historical setup and the presenter's personal reaction remain internal attribution, not our personal experience.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independently sourced FHD recording of the relevant Clock Tower 3 performance if rights and capture evidence permit, then our own grid character with a subtle and amplified gesture.
sections.transitionToNext: The visible exaggeration raises a medium-specific reason: some human cues do not reach the screen.

claims: A polygonal character cannot reproduce all the information a real person supplies.
A larger performance can compensate for missing cues.
Animation is authored representation, so physical subtlety alone does not guarantee that the intended meaning is communicated.
sections.observedVisuals: Clock Tower 3 performances continue while the source relates the director's reported reasoning.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep the information-loss argument, independently paraphrased. Do not reproduce the attributed quote or assert the quotation's primary provenance beyond what this lesson reports.
additionalPrerequisites: Identify concrete visible cues—body direction, silhouette, facial detail—before using the abstract phrase information loss. Our controlled example demonstrates reduced visible detail; it must not claim to measure human perception.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Keep one rig and gesture on the grid. Reduce its displayed size/detail, show which small cues become hard to distinguish, then increase the gesture amplitude while keeping duration constant.
sections.transitionToNext: The same loss explains why recording a human movement does not automatically finish the game animation.

claims: Motion-capture data generally needs adaptation rather than being dropped unchanged into a game.
How much amplification helps depends on the game's genre and intended performance.
sections.observedVisuals: Clock Tower 3 action footage continues through the motion-capture explanation.
additionalPrerequisites: Define motion capture as recording an actor's motion to drive a character, separate from hand-adjusting the resulting animation.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Compare a rights-cleared capture-derived clip with our edited version on the same rig/camera. Label source and editing truthfully; never call a keyframed stock clip raw motion capture without provenance.
sections.transitionToNext: Even after the same animation is prepared, the camera can change how much of it survives.

claims: A close view can make subtle animation legible.
The same subtlety may become insufficient when the character occupies less screen space or is farther from the camera.
sections.observedVisuals: Clock Tower 3 shots use varying character prominence while the narration discusses distance.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Same motion and rig, two camera distances on one grid. Then alter only amplitude in the small view. Use a fixed comparison scale or measured pixel height from our scene instead of an invented readability score.
sections.transitionToNext: Screen size is one constraint; the game's action rhythm and feel are the other constraints on the performance.

claims: Action games differ in back-and-forth, input feel and intended impact.
A literal sword swing may not carry enough expression for the action's role.
Deliberate broad movement often communicates the intended action more strongly.
sections.observedVisuals: Ultra Street Fighter IV shows Dan against Ryu; Elden Ring shows a sword action.
exampleRoles: Fighting-game performance connects exaggeration to action readability.
A weapon action broadens the principle beyond the initial cutscene case.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep the move from cutscene acting to interactive action. Do not substitute an unrelated animation-effects montage or change this into a universal rule that every game must exaggerate equally.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Separate independent FHD examples for the fighting and weapon-action roles, with overlays pointing to actual shoulder/weapon/body changes; our grid shot isolates the amplitude variable.
sections.transitionToNext: These examples support a practical criterion, rather than a ranking of old and new graphics.

claims: Clock Tower 3 is useful as an expressive-animation reference, not proof that its era is better.
Compensate for missing information with a performance sized for the character's presence, camera scale and controls.
sections.observedVisuals: Return to Clock Tower 3 performances, then the closing presenter statement.
sections.retainedTeaching: Do not add a defensive digression. Preserve the useful scope conditions in the conclusion while omitting nonessential comparison rhetoric.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Conclude on the same small-screen gesture before/after, showing how the action remains legible when detail is lost.

omissionsAndReasons.content: Presenter identity, grab-bag framing, personal admiration, director biography and source end card
omissionsAndReasons.reason: Nonessential attribution/history; preserve the observable Clock Tower 3 example and its information-loss reasoning.
Use the transferable concept in independent wording; retain reported attribution internally rather than copying the quote or claiming personal recollection.
